item.title: The US-Israel Relationship Is Shifting. Not Nearly Enough.
item.description: Benjamin Netanyahu says the end of US military aid to Israel marks a move “from dependency to an alliance of equals.” But ending military aid won’t stop the arms pipeline between Israel and Washington.
item.content:encoded:
On November 3, the very day of the midterm congressional elections, Donald Trump announced that the United States would cease its annual military aid to Israel at the end of this year. That aid, amounting to $3.8 billion annually, was provided under an agreement signed by the Obama administration in 2016, covering the ten years from 2019 through 2028. Trump cannot end it on his own — the money is appropriated by Congress — but the announcement was no surprise: it had been signaled before, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, now leading a caretaker government after Israel’s October election, said he was fine with it (or pretended to be), arguing that the Zionist state no longer needs this money and is perfectly capable of purchasing US weapons at its own expense.

The truth is that US military aid to Israel, as to other countries — regional states like Egypt and Jordan in particular — consists essentially of funding those governments’ purchase of US weaponry. In other words, it is an old and familiar method of using American taxpayers’ money to fund and enrich the military-industrial complex, one of the largest sectors of American capitalism.

The regular annual aid to Israel, moreover, is only a floor: Washington readily raises the amount when circumstances call for it. A report published last year found that the United States provided Israel with $21.7 billion in military aid during the first two years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, under the Biden and then the Trump administrations. That is but one measure of Washington’s full complicity in the genocide.

Still, the talk of ending the annual aid is significant, particularly given the timing. Everyone understood that, by making the announcement on Election Day, the president was attempting to mitigate the considerable damage done to his party by his enthusiastic support for Israel and his constant praise of Netanyahu at a time when the war on Gaza has shifted American public opinion, which is outraged at the spectacle of Israeli cruelty toward the Palestinians.

A Washington Post–Ipsos poll conducted last July revealed that 55 percent of the public now considers US military aid to Israel excessive, including 29 percent who support ending it completely, while 26 percent wish to see it reduced. According to another poll conducted last September, the proportion of those favorable to Israel in US public opinion has plummeted to 29 percent, its lowest level to date, while 59 percent declare holding an unfavorable view. And another recent poll, published last July, shows that 58 percent of young Americans under thirty (including 72 percent of young Democrats) sympathize with the Palestinian people nowadays, compared to 32 percent who sympathize with their Israeli oppressor.

These figures make inevitable a shift in the relationship between the Zionist state and its US godfather. The question is, what will be the nature of this shift? Netanyahu has boasted that the end of the funding marks a transition from dependency to an alliance of equals. The truth is that Israel would benefit from reducing its dependence on Washington, freeing itself as much as possible from the looming prospect of US pressure. That concern is all the more pressing for Israel given the shift in American public opinion and the Republicans’ debacle in the midterms, which cost them control of both houses of Congress.

One should not, however, be overly optimistic about the future of the relationship. The share of leftists among congressional Democrats has grown to an unprecedented degree, but the Democratic majority does not share their principled position: refusing to supply the Zionist state with US weapons at all, even at its own expense — or at least restricting the kind of weapons supplied and imposing strict conditions on their use, on Israel’s conduct in the Palestinian territories occupied in 1967 and, more generally, on its aggressive and expansionist regional policies.

A glimpse of where the Democratic majority’s position on Israel might be heading, should current trends continue, is offered by a policy agenda that J Street, the liberal Zionist lobby, published this November. Founded in 2008 as a rival to the much older, right-wing American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose origins date to 1954, J Street has gained significant influence at its rival’s expense over the past two years. Its proposal calls for treating Israel like any other wealthy ally — selling it weapons rather than subsidizing them. It still supports supplying Israel with defensive missiles like the Iron Dome, the product of cooperation between the US and Israeli military-industrial complexes, a collaboration J Street sees no problem with — so long as Israel pays.

As for the political conditions J Street would impose on the Israeli government, they include support for “elements” of the Gaza “peace plan” that the Trump administration produced last year — with an emphasis on disarming Hamas on the one hand and freezing the expansion of Zionist settlements in the West Bank on the other. The document also calls on Israel to commit to the prospect of a “State of Palestine” alongside it. That has nominally been Washington’s policy for years, including Trump’s: the plan drafted by Jared Kushner and unveiled by the president in January 2020, the final year of his first term, in Netanyahu’s presence and to his effusive praise.

Of course, even a shift in US policy in such a direction, should it occur, would have a beneficial impact despite its obvious limitations. But US foreign policy is primarily managed by the president, meaning that Trump will continue to shape it for the remaining two years of his term. Left-wing pressure for a radical change in US policy toward Israel must continue and grow, in public opinion and in Congress, building on the ongoing momentum — to stop the United States from arming Israel and to force a fundamental change in its treatment of the Palestinian people.

Deepening the shift in US policy toward Israel is a prerequisite for a change among Israeli Jews, and reversing the drift to the far right that has dominated their society since the turn of the century and accelerated dangerously after the Hamas-led operation of October 7, 2023. Without that change, there can be no relief for the Palestinian people from the unbearable suffering inflicted on them and no real prospect of their achieving their fundamental, inalienable right to self-determination — without which no durable peace is possible in the Middle East.
